1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a solid pawn pair on d5 and e6 and refuses to be pushed around. The cost is a light-squared bishop hemmed in by its own e-pawn; in return Black gets a sturdy position and aims for equality through patient manoeuvring.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, which will control e4 and d5 from a distance instead of occupying the centre with pawns. This stops White's e4 plan, frees the bishop from behind the e6 pawn and keeps Black flexible.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5.strategy: Hits d4 at once and asks White what to do with the centre. Black accepts an unbalanced game: if White gains space by advancing the d-pawn, Black gets a queenside pawn majority and play against the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+.name: Bogo-Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+.background: Named after Efim Bogoljubow, who is believed to have originated it and played it regularly in the 1920s. Nimzowitsch, Keres, Petrosian, Larsen, Smyslov and Korchnoi later adopted it.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+.strategy: Develops with check and asks White how to block. Black is ready to exchange the bishop for the blocking piece or retreat it, content with a compact, solid game. White gets the space and the choice of structure, but Black has few weaknesses.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 a6.name: Indian Defence: Dzindzi-Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that prepares ...b5 to attack the c4 pawn and win queenside space. It develops nothing and does not address the centre, so White gets time to build a full centre at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Ne4.name: Indian Defence: Döry Indian
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Ne4.background: Uncommon, but in 1937 it was the subject of a theme tournament in Vienna, won by Paul Keres.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Ne4.strategy: Takes the e4 square before White can occupy it with a pawn and pulls the knight toward the centre. It moves the same piece twice, though, and a developing move or the queen can hit the knight, so Black risks losing time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2.strategy: The most common answer: the bishop meets the check on a natural developing square and attacks the b4 bishop, so Black has to decide what to do with it. White keeps the pawn structure intact and a flexible development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: Grünfeld Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2.strategy: An ambitious interposition aiming to trade the knight for the bishop or force it back. The knight blocks the c1-bishop and is pinned against the king until White castles, a cost that must be repaid by a smooth development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nc3.strategy: Steps into the pinning set-up that arises after 3.Nc3 Bb4, by a different move order. White accepts that the knight can be pinned and the pawns doubled, and aims for a broad centre and the bishop pair in return.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nfd2.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: New England Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nfd2.strategy: Retreats the knight to d2, undoing a developing move and blocking the c1-bishop. It keeps the b1-knight free for c3 and supports e4, but White spends time on it and Black gets an easy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Qe7.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: Nimzowitsch Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Qe7.background: Now the most frequently played reply to 4.Bd2.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Qe7.strategy: Defends the bishop with the queen instead of trading it: if White takes on b4, the queen recaptures with check. Black keeps the tension and the choice of when to give up the bishop, at the price of an early queen move.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Bxd2+.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: Exchange Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Bxd2+.background: Not particularly popular, but played frequently by Ulf Andersson, often as a drawing line.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Bxd2+.strategy: The simplest solution: Black trades the bishop at once, and White recaptures. Black gets a solid, safe position with few risks, but also little to play for.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 c5.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: Vitolins Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 c5.strategy: Black strikes at d4 at once. If White takes on b4, the recapture doubles Black's pawns and pulls a pawn from the centre, but the pawn on b4 denies White's knight the c3 square.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 a5.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: Wade-Smyslov Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 a5.background: David Bronstein tried it as a sharper alternative.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 a5.strategy: Defends the bishop with a pawn and grabs queenside space. The price is a set of structural weaknesses on the queenside, so Black must make the bishop's outpost count.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Nc6.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: Haiti Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Nc6.strategy: Defends the bishop with a developing move, but the knight blocks the c-pawn, so Black can no longer challenge d4 with ...c5. White keeps the broader centre and carries on developing, while Black has nothing special to show for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7.name: Bogo-Indian Defence: Retreat Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 Be7.strategy: Retreats and so loses time, but White's bishop is not ideally placed on d2, where it blocks the queen's knight, which makes up part of it. A solid, slightly passive set-up that leaves White the choice of the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 a5 5.g.strategy: Fianchettoes and goes for the long diagonal instead of dealing with the bishop on b4 at once. Black's a-pawn has gained space but weakened the b5 square, and White develops quietly with the long diagonal in view.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 a5 5.e.strategy: Supports d4 and opens the f1-bishop for calm, natural development. If Black trades on d2, White recaptures with a developing move and keeps a comfortable game with a slight lead in the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 a5 5.N.strategy: Develops the knight and prepares to answer ...Bxc3 with the bishop. White keeps more central space, but the recapturing bishop can be challenged by a knight jumping to e4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 a5 5.g.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto: Black's bishop on b4 is held by the a-pawn, and the queen's bishop will come to b7 to fight for e4 and d5 alongside the f6 knight.

Castles at once and gets the king safe before the centre opens, while the a-pawn keeps the bishop on b4 in place against the d2 bishop. Black has not yet decided on the set-up for the other pieces, so the move keeps every plan open: natural, flexible and sound.

Takes a share of the centre with a pawn and attacks the c4 pawn, which has no defender yet, so White must deal with it. The structure is solid, but the c8 bishop stays hemmed in behind the e6 pawn and Black has committed the centre early; sound, a little passive.
Completes White's own fianchetto, which prepares to castle and opposes the long diagonal that Black's bishop will take. White keeps solid and waits to decide how to meet the pressure on d4 and c4.

Develops the knight to its natural square and invites the trade on c3. White recaptures with the d2 bishop and keeps a sound structure, but gains nothing special either: Black completes the set-up and equalises without trouble.

Covers c4 and e4 and keeps the queen flexible, but spends a move on the queen while Black completes the fianchetto and castles. White keeps a sound position without any pressure, and Black can trade off the b4 bishop whenever it likes.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 a5 5.g.name: Queen's Indian Defence: Yates Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Bd2 a5 5.g.strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the two bishops face each other on the long diagonal. Black has gained queenside space with the a-pawn and plans to trade the b4 bishop for a knight when it reaches c3, which strengthens the grip on the light squares.

Castles before settling the structure: the king is safe, the rook is ready for the centre, and the a-pawn still holds the b4 bishop. Black waits to see how White arranges the pieces, and the position stays sound and balanced.

Trades the dark-squared bishops at once. The a-pawn has gained queenside space, and White recaptures with a knight or the queen. Black gives up the bishop that pressed on the queenside, and the position becomes simple, with level chances and fewer ideas for both sides.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2 b6.strategy: Develops the fianchetto at once and leaves the knight on d2 pinned: it cannot move without exposing the king, and the b7-bishop will take over the long diagonal. White has to find a way to resolve the pin.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2 O-O.strategy: Castles at once and leaves the d2 knight pinned to the king, so White has to find a way out before developing freely. Black delays the choice of set-up for the queen's bishop and keeps both the fianchetto and a central pawn plan available: safe and flexible.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn and attacks c4, which the pinned d2 knight cannot guard. White must unpin or support the pawn first, and Black reaches a solid pawn structure; the price is that the c8 bishop stays hemmed in behind the e6 pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2 b6 5..strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once, before Black can add ...Bb7 and castle. If Black takes on d2, White recaptures and owns the two bishops; if the bishop retreats, White has gained queenside space.
Keeps the position solid and frees the f1-bishop, but leaves the pin on the d2 knight in place. Black decides when to trade bishop for knight, which hands White the bishop pair.

Adds protection to the pinned d2 knight and covers e4, but does nothing about the pin itself and spends a move while Black completes the fianchetto and castles. White can still ask the bishop later; sound, but it hands Black the initiative.
Takes the knight at once, so White's a3 has only forced a trade of Black's bishop for a knight. Black gives up the bishop pair, but the pin is gone and the position is simplified and equal.

Keeps the bishop by retreating, but White's a3 has gained a tempo for free and the bishop now sits on a passive square. White can build a full centre at leisure, while Black has saved the bishop from the trade at the price of time.

Retreats to a square where a pawn advance hits it: after e4, the threat of e5 would attack the bishop and the f6 knight at once, so Black loses another tempo. The bishop is kept, but White gets a free hand in the centre.

Recaptures with the queen, which keeps the pawn structure and the bishop pair. The queen on d2 stands in front of the c1-bishop, so White has to untangle that before the bishops take effect, but no knight is committed.

Recaptures with the c1 bishop, which develops it in the same move and keeps the pawn structure and both bishops. The price is the square: the bishop stands in front of the queen on d2 and needs a further move to find a better post. White keeps the bishop pair and a sound, level position.

Recaptures with the f3 knight, so the queen and the pawns stay put, but the knight just developed returns to d2, where it blocks the c1 bishop. White keeps the two bishops and an eye on e4, yet spends time on the knight while Black develops freely.

Completes the fianchetto: the bishop looks at the f3 knight and the long diagonal, and with the dark-squared bishop gone Black relies on piece control of e4 and d5. White has the bishop pair and the broader pawn centre; the fight is whether that centre can be undermined.

Castles before committing the queen's bishop: the king is safe and the rook stands ready for the centre. With the dark-squared bishop gone, Black relies on piece pressure on e4 and d5, while White has the two bishops and the freer pawn centre; the fight is whether Black can undermine that centre.

Contests the centre with a pawn at once and gives the position a solid frame. But the pawn on d5 blocks the long diagonal that the b6 pawn was meant to open for the queen's bishop, and White keeps the two bishops and can open the centre with a trade on d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2 b6 5..name: Queen's Indian Defence, with e3, Bb4+ Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 Bb4+ 4.Nbd2 b6 5..strategy: Completes the fianchetto: the bishop looks down the long diagonal at e4, d5 and the knight on f3, while the bishop on b4 keeps White's d2 knight pinned to the king. Black has a compact set-up, and White must find a way to untangle the pieces.

Castles and keeps the pin on the d2 knight, so White still has to untangle its pieces. Black leaves the choice of square for the queen's bishop open until it has seen how White arranges the pieces: a safe, flexible move that is in no hurry.

Trades the bishop for the knight at once, before White's pawn can force the issue. White recaptures and has the two bishops, but Black gets a solid, compact position and develops easily; a tidy but unambitious way to ease the game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5.strategy: Settles the tension on d4 by taking space: the pawn on d5 cramps Black's pieces and prepares a broad centre. In return Black gets a half-open e-file, a queenside pawn majority and plenty of counterplay, so White has to keep the centre under control.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and keeps the centre flexible instead of committing to a pawn advance. If Black trades on d4, White recaptures with a knight and gets quick development and control of d5 with the c4 pawn; White has not yet fixed the pawn structure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.e3.strategy: Solid but modest: it supports the d4 pawn and opens the diagonal of the f1 bishop, but claims no space. Black can trade pawns in the centre or build up with the d-pawn and equalises easily; White has chosen a quiet game over the space grab.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 exd5.strategy: The principal answer: Black opens the e-file and, after the recapture, has a queenside pawn majority against White's central pawns. The game becomes a clear contest between White's space in the centre and Black's active pieces and queenside play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5.name: Blumenfeld Countergambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5.background: Named after the Russian master Benjamin Blumenfeld, who invented it; World Champion Alexander Alekhine played it later.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5.strategy: A pawn sacrifice that attacks White's centre from the flank. Black wants to build a strong central pawn mass, develop quickly and play against the king's side, and pays a wing pawn for it. The game is sharp and double-edged.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 d6.strategy: A quiet move that guards the c5 pawn and frees the c8 bishop, preparing a solid pawn structure. It leaves White to decide the centre, by capturing on e6 or by keeping the space on d5, and Black is left with a safe but slightly passive game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.Bg5.name: Blumenfeld Countergambit: Duz-Khotimirsky Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop with a pin on the f6 knight against the queen, and declines to grab anything. White keeps the pawn on d5 and a space advantage, and leaves Black to decide how to resolve the tension. It is White's most popular reply.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.dxe6.strategy: Takes the pawn on e6 and accepts the gambit. White gives up the central pawn that cramped Black and lets the f-file open, hoping to keep the extra queenside pawn; Black gets quick development and a strong centre in return.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.a4.strategy: Attacks the b5 pawn with the rook's pawn, trying to undermine the gambit pawn before Black's pieces come out. It develops nothing and leaves the tension on e6 untouched, so Black has several comfortable answers; White keeps the space on d5 but gains nothing concrete.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.Bg5.strategy: Takes on d5 at once and ends the tension in the centre. After White recaptures, the b5 pawn is no longer attacked, so the gambit costs Black nothing. Black has a queenside majority, but the f6 knight is still pinned to the queen.

Moves the attacked pawn forward, keeping the gambit pawn and gaining queenside space. The pawn on b4 takes the c3 square away from White's b1 knight, but Black leaves the pin on f6 and the tension on e6 unresolved, so the game stays sharp.

Develops the bishop and eyes d5, but leaves the pin on f6 and the tension in the centre as they are. White uses the time to take the centre with e4 while the knight stays pinned, so the gambit gives Black no compensation.

Recaptures towards the centre, which also ends the attack on b5, so material is level. White has a pawn on d5 and space, Black a queenside majority and active pieces; the pinned knight on f6 is the first thing Black has to solve.

Takes the b-pawn and leaves the black pawn on d5 standing, so material is level but Black keeps a broad pawn centre. The queen can check on a5 with tempo, and White has to look after the b5 pawn; riskier than recapturing on d5.

Develops the knight and adds attackers to both b5 and d5, keeping the pressure on Black's pawns. Black has to react straight away and the position becomes sharp, with the pinned knight on f6 central to the tactics; playable, but harder for White to control than recapturing.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.Bg5.name: Blumenfeld Countergambit: Spielmann Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.Bg5.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop at once and so deals with the pin on the f6 knight. If White trades on f6, Black recaptures with the queen, which then eyes the long diagonal towards b2; if the bishop retreats, Black has spent a tempo but keeps its knight and solid centre.

Supports the c5 pawn and frees the c8 bishop, preparing a solid set-up around the pawn centre. Black accepts White's space on d5 and plays on the queenside, where it has a pawn majority, and deals with the pinned f6 knight later.

Unpins the knight, but loses material at once: d6 attacks the bishop, and taking the pawn fails to Qxd6, because the d7 pawn blocks Black's queen from recapturing. Black gives up a piece for a pawn at best.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.dxe6.strategy: Recaptures with the f-pawn, which opens the f-file for the rook and keeps the d-pawn at home for a stand in the centre. The price is a looser pawn cover around the king, and the b5 pawn is still left hanging to White's c-pawn.

Recaptures with the d-pawn, which opens the d-file: White trades queens by taking on d8 with check, takes the b5 pawn and is a clean pawn up. Black has no compensation, since the king has lost castling and there is no initiative left.

Takes the c-pawn at once instead of recapturing on e6, leaving White's e6 pawn alive. After exf7+ Kxf7 the king stands in the open, cannot castle and has lost its e- and f-pawns; a dubious way to regain the pawn.

Takes the gambit pawn and leaves White a pawn up. White's problem is holding it: Black's central pawns and open f-file give Black rapid development, and White must give the pawn back or survive the initiative.

Opens the f1 bishop so that a capture on c4 is met by a recapture on c4. White declines to keep the extra pawn and plays for solid development instead, leaving Black the open f-file and a flexible centre; sound, but White gives up the most ambitious option.

Develops the knight but gives up the chance to take the gambit pawn: Black can hit the knight with ...b4 or capture on c4, so White gains no time. The position stays level, but White passes up the extra pawn on offer.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.dxe6.name: Blumenfeld Countergambit Accepted
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 b5 5.dxe6.strategy: Stakes out the whole centre with pawns on c5, d5 and e6, and frees both bishops for development. Black is a pawn down and plays for the initiative: the compensation is space, quick development and pressure on the open f-file.

Challenges the b5 pawn at once. If White takes on a6, the bishop recaptures with pressure on the e2 pawn and the a-file is half open for the rook; Black is still a pawn down but develops quickly. White can also decline to take and keep the pawn on b5, which costs time.

Develops the bishop and attacks the knight on f3 along the long diagonal; the knight is well defended, but a trade would damage White's pawns. The move keeps ...d5 in reserve and lets White consolidate; playable, but slower than staking out the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.cx.strategy: Recaptures towards the centre: White has a space-gaining pawn on d5 and a half-open c-file against the c5 pawn, while Black has the e-file and a queenside majority. Both sides get a clear plan: White presses in the centre, Black counterattacks on the wing.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.Nc.strategy: Develops a piece but ignores the pawn White is missing. Black keeps it by pushing the d-pawn forward, which hits the knight and gains space, or by taking on c4; either way White is a pawn down with little to show for it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.Qx.strategy: Loses the queen for a knight: the knight on f6 takes it, and White's c-pawn can only win the knight back. Recapturing with the pawn is the only way to regain the pawn safely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.cx.strategy: Shields the c5 pawn, stops the d-pawn from advancing and frees the c8 bishop. Black commits to a firm pawn chain and gives up the idea of an early central break; the game is a manoeuvring fight against White's space.

Offers the b-pawn to open lines against White's queenside, but there is nothing behind it. White builds the centre with e4 while Black's king is still in the middle, and the sacrifice does not pay for itself.

Develops the bishop quickly, but on d6 it blocks Black's own d-pawn. White can build a big pawn centre, and the pawn on d5 keeps Black cramped, so White has a lasting space advantage rather than a small edge.
Brings the knight to defend the d5 pawn and to back up a central advance. White develops with a purpose, keeping the space it has gained, and now Black has to find counterplay against a solid centre.

Claims the full centre at once and opens the way for quick development and castling. The cost is a half-open e-file for Black to press on. Grabbing the pawn with ...Nxe4 fails: Qa4+ checks the king and attacks the knight, so White wins it.

Fianchettoes the king's bishop, which guards the king and will cover d5 and e4 once the knight on f3 moves, for a slow and solid game. White aims to reroute that knight to c4; the set-up offers Black few targets, but also puts little immediate pressure on Black.

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.cx.name: Benoni Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.cx.background: The name comes from Aaron Reinganum's 1825 book Ben-Oni, which analysed 1.d4 c5, then an unknown opening. It later attached itself to openings in which Black answers d4 with an early ...c5, including 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5.
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 c5 4.d5 exd5 5.cx.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop so that it presses along the long diagonal against White's centre and queenside. Black accepts a cramped position for active piece play and the queenside majority, while White aims for a central break.

Prepares ...b5, the usual queenside plan, and is sound, but White's a4 answers it: ...b5 axb5 axb5 loses the unprotected rook on a8 to Rxa8. Black's counterplay is delayed a move and the position stays cramped.
Develops the bishop to e7 and prepares castling, a solid but passive set-up. The bishop does not bear on White's centre as a fianchettoed bishop does, so White builds a full centre at leisure.
